## Abstract

The Relative Neighborhood Graph (RNG) of a set of nk-dimensional points connects “relatively close” neighbors: two points are connected by an edge if they are at least as close to each other as to any other point. Toussaint recently investigated the properties of the RNG in the Euclidean metric and proposed algorithms for its computation. This note examines one of the open problems listed by Toussaint: the extension of the analysis to non-Euclidean metrics. It is shown that Bentley's range query data structures may be used to improve the speed of the best known RNG algorithm in the L_{∞} (for k ⩾ 2) and L_{1} (for k = 2) metrics.

L8@P0: Abstract
L9@P0: The general position number gp(G) of a connected graph G is the cardinality
L10@P0: of a largest set S of vertices such that no three pairwise distinct vertices from S
L11@P0: lie on a common geodesic. It is proved that gp(G) ≥ ω(GSR, where GSR is the
L12@P0: strong resolving graph of G, and ω(GSR) is its clique number. That the bound is
L13@P0: sharp is demonstrated with numerous constructions including for instance direct
L14@P0: products of complete graphs and different families of strong products, of generalized
L15@P0: lexicographic products, and of rooted product graphs. For the strong product it is
L16@P0: proved that gp(G ⊠ H) ≥ gp(G)gp(H), and asked whether the equality holds for
L17@P0: arbitrary connected graphs G and H. It is proved that the answer is in particular
L18@P0: positive for strong products with a complete factor, for strong products of complete
L19@P0: bipartite graphs, and for certain strong cylinders.
L20@P0: E-mails: sandi.klavzar@fmf.uni-lj.si, ismael.gonzalez@uca.es
L21@P0: Key words: general position problem; strong resolving graph; graph products
L22@P0: AMS Subj. Class.: 05C12, 05C76
L23@P0: 1 Introduction
L24@P0: The general position problem was recently and independently introduced in [7, 14]. If
L25@P0: G = (V (G), E(G)) is a graph, then S ⊆ V (G) is a general position set if no triple of
L26@P0: vertices from S lie on a common geodesic in G. The general position problem is to
L27@P0: find a largest general position set of G, the order of such a set is the general position
L28@P0: number gp(G) of G. A general position set of G of order gp(G) is shortly called gp-set.
L29@P0: The general position problem has been further studied in a sequence of very recent
L30@P0: papers [1, 2, 8, 10].
L31@P0: A vertex u of a connected graph G is maximally distant from a vertex v if every
L32@P0: w ∈ N(u) satisfies dG(v, w) ≤ dG(u, v), where N(u) is the open neighborhood of u. If
L33@P0: u is maximally distant from v, and v is maximally distant from u, then u and v are
L34@P0-1: 1mutually maximally distant (MMD for short). The strong resolving graph GSR of G
L35@P1: has V (G) as the vertex set, two vertices being adjacent in GSR if they are MMD in G.
L36@P1: The notion of the strong resolving graph was introduced in [9] as a tool to study the
L37@P1: strong metric dimension. It was proved that the problem of finding the strong metric
L38@P1: dimension of a graph G can be transformed to the problem of finding the vertex cover
L39@P1: number of GSR. Further on, the strong resolving graph itself was remarked as a kind
L40@P1: of graph transformation in [6], and several characterizations and realizations of it were
L41@P1: described.
L42@P1: Now, one of the open problems presented in [6] concerns finding applications for the
L43@P1: strong resolving graph construction, other than that of computing the strong metric
L44@P1: dimension of graphs. In this paper we give a partial answer to this problem by establishing a connection between the general position number of a graph G and the
L45@P1: clique number of the graph GSR. More precisely, in Theorem 3.1 we prove that
L46@P1: gp(G) ≥ ω(GSR) holds for any connected graph G. Then we demonstrate with different infinite families of graphs, including direct products of complete graphs, that the
L47@P1: bound is sharp. We also show that for any integers r ≥ t ≥ 2, there exists a graph
L48@P1: G such that gp(G) = r and ω(GSR) = t. In Section 4 we focus on strong products
L49@P1: of graphs. We prove that gp(G ⊠ H) ≥ gp(G)gp(H) holds for connected graphs G
L50@P1: and H and that the bound is again sharp. In particular, if gp(G) = ω(GSR), then
L51@P1: gp(G ⊠ Kn) = n · gp(G) = ω((G ⊠ Kn)SR). We close the section with a question on
L52@P1: whether actually the equality gp(G ⊠ H) = gp(G)gp(H) holds for arbitrary connected
L53@P1: graphs G and H. In Section 5 we give additional large families of graphs, based on
L54@P1: the generalized lexicographic product, for which the equality in Theorem 3.1 holds. In
L55@P1: the final section we determine the general position number for different rooted product
L56@P1: graphs and relate the values with the corresponding clique numbers of strong resolving
L57@P1: graphs.
L58@P1: Before giving our results, we list in the next section definitions and concepts not
L59@P1: yet given, as well as some results needed later.

L134@P2-3: 33 The lower bound and equality cases
L135@P3: In this section we first prove the key result that connects the general position problem
L136@P3: with the strong resolving graphs.
L137@P3: Theorem 3.1 If G is a connected graph, then gp(G) ≥ ω(GSR). Moreover, equality
L138@P3: holds if and only if G contains a gp-set that induces a complete subgraph of GSR.
L139@P3: Proof. Let S ⊆ V (GSR) induce a complete subgraph of GSR. This means that any two
L140@P3: vertices x, y ∈ S are MMD in G. We now consider the vertices of S in the graph G. If
L141@P3: there are three distinct vertices x, y, z ∈ S lying on a common geodesic, say y lies in an
L142@P3: x, z-geodesic, then neither x, y nor y, z are MMD in G, which is a contradiction. Thus,
L143@P3: any three vertices of S do not lie in a common geodesic of G, and therefore, S is a
L144@P3: general position set in G. Selecting S to be a complete subgraph GSR of order ω(GSR)
L145@P3: leads to the desired bound.
L146@P3: Suppose now that gp(G) = ω(GSR). By the above, any complete subgraph of GSR of
L147@P3: order ω(GSR) yields a gp-set. Conversely, let S be a gp-set of G that forms a complete
L148@P3: subgraph of GSR. Then, using the already proven inequality gp(G) ≥ ω(GSR), we have
L149@P3: |S| ≤ ω(GSR) ≤ gp(G) = |S| ,
L150@P3: from which we conclude that ω(GSR) = gp(G). 

L152@P3: equality in Theorem 3.1. However, such a characterization seems to be elusive because of the great variety of different structures that can appear. In the following we

L154@P3: previously.
L155@P3: • Block graphs, in particular complete graphs and trees.
L156@P3: Indeed, in [7] it was observed that in block graphs the set of simplicial vertices
L157@P3: forms a gp-set. Since simplicial vertices of a graph G also form a set of MMD
L158@P3: vertices of a graph (equivalently, they form a complete subgraph of GSR), Theorem 3.1 implies that gp(G) = ω(GSR) if G is a block graph.
L159@P3: • Complete multipartite graphs.

several researchers working on applying graph theory to mathematical modeling
of chemical phenomena. The molecular graph or chemical graph gives a graph-
theoretical representation of a molecule and provides valuable information into
the chemical phenomena. The atoms of a molecule are represented by vertices or
nodes and the edges of the graph stand for the covalent bonds among the atoms.
A class of highly branched molecules, called dendrimers [9] are known to be suit-
able for a number of biomedical applications. Many of the structural properties
of a molecular graphs have been studied in terms of topological indices that are
numeric quantities developed as molecular descriptors. Weiner-Index [12] is one
of the earliest topological indices introduced by Weiner in connection with mod-

[5, 8] ) have been introduced and investigated subsequently. The eccentric con-
nectivity index is a parameter recently introduced [10] and subsequently studied
(see for example [2, 6, 7, 11, 13]) with regard to physical / biological properties
of molecules.

## Abstract

It is revealed from the previous studies that there is a strong relation between the chemical characteristic of a chemical compound and its molecular structure. Topological indices defined on the molecular structure of biomolecules can help to gain a better understanding of their physical features and biological activities. Eccentricity connectivity indices are distance-based molecular structure descriptors that have been used for the mathematical modeling of biological activities of diverse nature. As the porphyrin has photofunctional properties, such as a large absorption cross-section, fluorescence emission, and photosensitizing properties, due to these properties, porphyrin dendrimers can be used as photofunctional nanodevices. In this paper, we compute the exact formulae of different versions of eccentric connectivity index and their corresponding polynomials for a class of porphyrin-cored dendrimers. The results obtained can be used in computer-aided molecular design methods applied to pharmaceutical engineering.

Keywords: porphyrin-cored dendrimers, eccentric connectivity index, total eccentric connectivity index, augmented eccentric connectivity index

## 1. Introduction

In this era of rapid technological development, a large number of new nanomaterials, crystalline materials, and drugs emerge every year. To determine the chemical properties of such a large number of new compounds and new drugs requires a large amount of chemical experiments, thereby greatly increasing the workload of the chemical and pharmaceutical researchers. In this regard, computing different types of topological indices has provided the insights into medicinal behaviour of several compounds and drugs [1,2]. The computation method of topological indices has proven its worth by yielding medical information of drugs with less use of chemical-related equipment [3,4].

L14@P0: Abstract
L15@P0: The strong resolving graph GSR of a connected graph G was introduced in [Discrete
L16@P0: Applied Mathematics 155 (1) (2007) 356–364] as a tool to study the strong metric dimension
L17@P0: of G. Basically, it was shown that the problem of finding the strong metric dimension of G
L18@P0: can be transformed to the problem of finding the vertex cover number of GSR. Since then,
L19@P0: several articles dealing with this subject have been published. In this paper, we survey the
L20@P0: state of knowledge on the strong resolving graph and also derive some new results.
L21@P0: Keywords: Strong resolving graph; strong metric dimension.
L22@P0: AMS Subject Classification Numbers: 05C76.
L23@P0: 1 Introduction
L24@P0: Graphs are basic combinatorial structures, and transformations of structures are fundamental to
L25@P0: the development of mathematics. Particularly, in graph theory, some elementary transformations
L26@P0: generate a new graph from an original one by some simple local changes, such as addition or
L27@P0: deletion of a vertex or of an edge, merging and splitting of vertices, edge contraction, etc. Other
L28@P0: advanced transformations create a new graph from the original one by complex changes, such as
L29@P0: complement graph, line graph, total graph, graph power, dual graph, strong resolving graph, etc.
L30@P0: Some of these transformations of graphs emerged as a natural tool to solve practical problems.
L31@P0: In other cases, the problem of finding a specific parameter of a graph has become the problem
L32@P0: of finding another parameter of another graph obtained from the original one. This is the case
L33@P0-1: 1of the strong resolving graph GSR of a connected graph G which was introduced by Oellermann
L34@P1: and Peters-Fransen in [31] as a tool to study the strong metric dimension of G. Basically, it
L35@P1: was shown that the problem of finding the strong metric dimension of G can be transformed to
L36@P1: the problem of finding the vertex cover number of GSR. Since then, several articles dealing with
L37@P1: the strong resolving graph have been published. However, in almost all these works the results
L38@P1: related to the strong resolving graph are not explicit, as they implicitly appear as a part of the
L39@P1: proofs of main results concerning the strong metric dimension. In this sense, this interesting
L40@P1: construction has passed in front of researchers’s eyes without the attention that should require.
L41@P1: In this paper, we make an attempt of motivating the community of graph theorists to have a
L42@P1: look into this direction and take more in consideration this construction. Accordingly, herein we
L43@P1: survey the state of knowledge on the strong resolving graph and also derive some new results.
L44@P1: For a graph transformation, there are two general problems [9], which we shall formulate in
L45@P1: terms of strong resolving graphs:
L46@P1: • Realization Problem.1 Determine which graphs have a given graph as their strong
L47@P1: resolving graphs.
L48@P1: • Characterization Problem. Characterize those graphs that are strong resolving graphs
L49@P1: of some graphs.
L50@P1: The majority of results presented in this paper concerns the above mentioned problems.
L51@P1: Basically, we focus on the following graph equation
L52@P1: GSR ∼= H, (1)
L53@P1: i.e., the goal is to find all pairs of graphs G and H satisfying (1).
L54@P1: The remainder of the paper is structured as follows. Subsection 1.1 covers general notation
L55@P1: and terminology. Subsection 1.2 is devoted to introduce the strong metric dimension, whereas
L56@P1: Subsection 1.3 introduces the strong resolving graph. In Section 2 we study the realization
L57@P1: problem for some specific families of graphs, while in Section 3 we collect the known results
L58@P1: related to the characterization problem of product graphs. We close our exposition with a
L59@P1: collection of open problems to be dealt with. In order to gain more completeness of this work,
L60@P1: we include or improve the proofs of some results which are remarkable for the topic, although
L61@P1: the main part of them are already published in some journals.

L115@P2: 1.2 Strong Metric Dimension of Graphs
L116@P2: A vertex w ∈ V (G) strongly resolves two different vertices u, v ∈ V (G) if dG(w, u) = dG(w, v) +
L117@P2: dG(v, u) or dG(w, v) = dG(w, u) + dG(u, v), i.e., there exists some shortest w − u path containing
L118@P2: v or some shortest w − v path containing u. A set S of vertices in a connected graph G is a
L119@P2-3: 3strong metric generator for G if every two vertices of G are strongly resolved by some vertex of S.
L120@P3: The smallest cardinality of a strong metric generator for G is called the strong metric dimension
L121@P3: and is denoted by dims(G). A strong metric basis of G is a strong metric generator for G of
L122@P3: cardinality dims(G).
L123@P3: Several researches on the strong metric dimension of graphs have recently been developed.
L124@P3: For instance, the trivial bounds 1 ≤ dims(G) ≤ n − 1 are known from the first works as well
L125@P3: as characterizations on whether they are tight. Moreover, it has been noticed that the strong
L126@P3: metric dimension of several graphs can be straightforwardly computed for some basic examples
L127@P3: which we next remark.
L128@P3: Observation 1.
L129@P3: (a) dims(G) = 1 if and only if G is isomorphic to the path Pn on n ≥ 2 vertices.
L130@P3: (b) dims(G) = n − 1 if and only if G is isomorphic to the complete graph Kn on n ≥ 2 vertices.
L131@P3: (c) For any cycle Cn of order n, dims(Cn) = ⌈n/2⌉.
L132@P3: (d) For any tree T with l(T) leaves, dims(T) = l(T) − 1.
L133@P3: (e) For any complete bipartite graph Kr,t, dims(Kr,t) = r + t − 2.
L134@P3: The strong metric dimension is a relatively new parameter (defined in 2004). Since then,
L135@P3: this parameter has been investigated for several classes of graphs. For instance, we cite the
L136@P3: works on Cartesian product graphs [19, 31, 34], Cartesian sum graphs [23], corona graphs [22],
L137@P3: direct product graphs [21, 34], strong product graphs [24], lexicographical product graphs [25],
L138@P3: Cayley graphs [31], Sierpi´nski graphs [33], distance-hereditary graphs [26], and convex polytopes
L139@P3: [16]. Also, some Nordhaus-Gaddum type results for the strong metric dimension of a graph
L140@P3: and its complement are known [39]. Besides the theoretical results related to the strong metric
L141@P3: dimension, a mathematical programming model [16] and metaheuristic approaches [17, 28] for
L142@P3: finding this parameter have been developed. Some complexity and approximation results are
L143@P3: also known from the works [31] and [4], respectively. On the other hand, a fractional version of
L144@P3: the strong metric dimension has been studied in [12, 13, 14]. In these three works the strong
L145@P3: resolving graph is also used as an important tool. For more information we refer the reader to
L146@P3: the survey [18] and the Ph.D. thesis [20].

L276@P6: addition, the characterization problem of graphs of diameter two is considered. We begin with
L277@P6: the characterization of graphs whose strong resolving graph is complete. To this end, we need

L11@P0: Abstract. Previous experiments with low dimensional data sets have shown
L12@P0: that Gabriel graph methods for instance-based learning are among the best machine learning algorithms for pattern classification applications. However, as
L13@P0: the dimensionality of the data grows large, all data points in the training set tend
L14@P0: to become Gabriel neighbors of each other, bringing the efficacy of this method
L15@P0: into question. Indeed, it has been conjectured that for high-dimensional data,
L16@P0: proximity graph methods that use sparser graphs, such as relative neighbor
L17@P0: graphs (RNG) and minimum spanning trees (MST) would have to be employed
L18@P0: in order to maintain their privileged status. Here the performance of proximity
L19@P0: graph methods, in instance-based learning, that employ Gabriel graphs, relative
L20@P0: neighborhood graphs, and minimum spanning trees, are compared experimentally on high-dimensional data sets. These methods are also compared empirically against the traditional k-NN rule and support vector machines (SVMs), the
L21@P0: leading competitors of proximity graph methods.
L22@P0: Keywords: Instance-based learning, Gabriel graph, relative neighborhood
L23@P0: graph (RNG), minimum spanning tree (MST), proximity graphs, support vector
L24@P0: machines (SVM), sequential minimal optimization (SMO), machine learning.
L25@P0: 1 Introduction
L26@P0: Instance-based learning algorithms are among the most attractive methods used today
L27@P0: in many applications of machine learning to a wide variety of pattern recognition
L28@P0: problems. The quintessential instance-based learning algorithm is the well-known kNearest Neighbor (k-NN) rule, whereby a new unknown pattern is classified into the
L29@P0: class most heavily represented among its k nearest neighbors present in the training
L30@P0: set. Two of the most attractive features of this method are immediately evident: (1) its
L31@P0-1: simplicity, and (2) the fact that no knowledge is required about the underlying distribution of the training data. Nevertheless, unanswered questions about the rule’s performance left doubts among its potential users. In 1967 Cover and Hart [4] showed  Proximity-Graph Instance-Based Learning, SVM, and High Dimensionality 223
L32@P1: that, under some continuity assumptions the number n of patterns in the training data
L33@P1: becomes infinite, the asymptotic probability of misclassification of the 1-NN rule is
L34@P1: at most twice the Bayes error. Furthermore Devroye showed that for all distributions,
L35@P1: the asymptotic probability of misclassification of the k-NN rule approaches the Bayes
L36@P1: error provided that k and n approach infinity, and the ratio k/n approaches zero [7-8].
L37@P1: These constraints are satisfied for example when k = n1/2. Thus the ultimate classificatory power of the k-NN rule was finally firmly established. Despite this great news,
L38@P1: resistance to using k-NN rules in practice persisted, fueled by several misconceptions,
L39@P1: one being that all n points must be stored, thus requiring too much storage. It was
L40@P1: pointed out in 1979 that the decision boundary of the 1-NN rule remains unchanged
L41@P1: when the data points surrounded by Voronoi neighbors of the same class are discarded (in parallel) [23-24]. A second false claim frequently encountered is that in
L42@P1: order to determine the nearest neighbor of an unknown query point X, the distances
L43@P1: between X and all the n points in the training data must be computed. Today there
L44@P1: exist a plethora of methods for avoiding such exhaustive search.
L45@P1: The above-mentioned false claims notwithstanding, in practice it is desired to reduce the size of the training set, or the concomitant memory of the data structure into
L46@P1: which the training set is embedded, as much as possible, while maintaining a low
L47@P1: probability of misclassification. Therefore much research has been devoted to this
L48@P1: topic, yielding a cornucopia of different approaches [20]. One elegant and promising
L49@P1: approach generalizes Voronoi (or Delaunay triangulation) editing [23] to incorporate
L50@P1: more general proximity graphs [24]. In the latter approach, for any definition of proximity, data points with the property that all their proximity-graph neighbors belong to
L51@P1: the same class are discarded (in parallel). Previous experiments with low-dimensional
L52@P1: data sets have shown that proximity graph methods that used the Gabriel graph were
L53@P1: among the best machine learning algorithms for pattern classification applications [2-
L54@P1: 3, 24, 28]. However, as the dimensionality of the data grows large, all data points in
L55@P1: the training set tend to become Gabriel neighbors of each other, effectively forsaking
L56@P1: the notion of proximity, and bringing the efficacy of this method into question [14].
L57@P1: We conjectured that for high-dimensional data, methods that use sparser graphs, such
L58@P1: as relative neighbor graphs (RNG) or minimum spanning trees (MST), would yield
L59@P1: better results by avoiding proximity-graphs with too many edges. In this paper we
L60@P1: conduct experiments that confirm this hypothesis.
L61@P1: Here the performance of various proximity graph methods for instance-based
L62@P1: learning is compared experimentally using Gabriel graphs, relative neighborhood
L63@P1: graphs, and minimum spanning trees, on a group of high-dimensional data sets. These

L100@P3: 3 Reducing the Size of the Training Data
L101@P3: The first published algorithm for reducing the size of the training data for use in nearest neighbor decision rules was the condensed nearest neighbor rule [12]. The purpose
L102@P3: of this algorithm was to discard as much data as possible by removing data points that
L103@P3: were “far” from the decision boundary, in a heuristic fashion, without knowing precisely where the decision boundary lay. However, although the condensed training set
L104@P3: discarded many points (one of its best features), and obtained zero misclassification
L105@P3: errors when classifying the original full training set, a property referred to as trainingset consistency, the performance on separate testing data was modest.
L106@P3: In 1972, Wilson [26] proposed an algorithm that did the exact opposite of Hart’s
L107@P3: algorithm, by discarding the data that were “near” the decision boundary, also in a
L108@P3: heuristic manner. This had the effect of “smoothing” the decision boundary. In the
L109@P3: pre-processing stage of Wilson’s edited nearest neighbor rule, all the data are first
L110@P3: classified using the k-NN rule in a leave-one-out setting, and all the data misclassified
L111@P3: are then discarded. In the decision stage new data are classified using the 1-NN rule
L112@P3: with the resulting (smaller) edited set. As would be expected, although this algorithm
L113@P3: does not remove much of the training data, its redeeming feature is that for a large
L114@P3: class of problems the asymptotic performance of the edited nearest neighbor rule is
L115@P3: difficult to differentiate from that of the optimal Bayes decision rule. In effect, Wilson’s editing scheme makes the 1-NN rule perform like the k-NN rule with the optimal value of k. This edited nearest neighbor decision rule has come to be known in the
L116@P3: literature as Wilson editing, and has left a lasting impact on subsequent instance-based
L117@P3: learning algorithms. Indeed, almost all algorithms proposed since 1972 use Wilson
L118@P3: editing as one of their initial steps, with the primary goal of lowering the final overall
L119@P3: probability of misclassification.
L120@P3: One of the best algorithms in the literature for considerably reducing the size of the
L121@P3: training set without degrading its classification performance is the iterative casefiltering algorithm (ICF) of Brighton and Mellish [1]. This algorithm consists of a
L122@P3: two-step procedure for discarding data. The first step is Wilson editing, in which the
L123@P3: k-NN rule is used to classify the data, in this case with k = 3. The second step is an
L124@P3: original condensing step that makes use of novel notions of reachable sets and coverage sets. New query points are then classified using the 1-NN rule with the resulting
L125@P3-4: condensed set. 226 G.T. Toussaint and C. Berzan
L126@P4: An omnipresent concern with the k-NN rule has been the selection of the value of k
L127@P4: that will yield the lowest probability of misclassification for the problem at hand.
L128@P4: Furthermore, in the traditional k-NN rule, once the value of k has been chosen it remains fixed for all subsequent classification decisions. Therefore, in this setting the kNN rule does not adapt its value of k to either the local density or the spatial distribution of the neighbors of a query point. Proximity graphs provide an approach that not
L129@P4: only takes care of these issues, but does so in a fully automatic way without having to
L130@P4: tune any parameters. Instead of taking a majority vote from among the k nearest
L131@P4: neighbors of a query point X, the proximity graph decision rule takes a majority vote
L132@P4: from among all the graph neighbors of X determined by a suitable proximity graph of
L133@P4: the training data. As a concrete example, consider the Delaunay triangulation of the
L134@P4: set of points in Figure 2 (left). It is evident that the number of Delaunay neighbors of
L135@P4: a point varies greatly depending on the point’s location. The leftmost point for example has only three neighbors, whereas the point in the center of the circularly arranged
L136@P4: group of points has thirteen neighbors. Similarly, the point in the upper right has eleven Delaunay neighbors, and furthermore these eleven do not even correspond to the
L137@P4: eleven nearest neighbors. Proximity graph methods may then replace the k-NN rule in
L138@P4: Wilson editing, thus dispensing with the problem of determining a suitable value of k.
L139@P4: Proximity graph methods may also be used for discarding points that are far from
L140@P4: the decision boundary, in condensing algorithms. The first condensing algorithm that
L141@P4: used proximity graphs employed the Delaunay triangulation [23]. In this algorithm a
L142@P4: data point X is first marked if all its Delaunay neighbors belong to the same class as
L143@P4: that of X. Then all marked points are deleted. The strength of this condensing method
L144@P4: lies in the fact that the 1-NN decision boundary of the original full training set is not
L145@P4: changed after the data are deleted, a property referred to as decision-boundary consistency. All the discarded data are completely redundant and hence do not play a role in
L146@P4: determining the decision boundary of the original larger training set. Initial experiments with Delaunay graph condensing, performed with cervical cancer data collected
L147@P4: at McGill University that consisted of two thousand cells in four dimensions [18],
L148@P4: revealed that the amount of data discarded was not particularly impressive [24]. An
L149@P4: effect of the curse-of-dimensionality is that even in a space of only four dimensions,
L150@P4: two thousand points are sufficiently scattered to allow points to have many Delaunay
L151@P4: neighbors. Clearly, a point with a greater number of neighbors has a higher probability that one of its neighbors belongs to a different class, especially if it lies near the
L152@P4: decision boundary, and thus a smaller probability that it will be discarded. This observation prompted the application of proximity graphs that have fewer edges than
L153@P4: the Delaunay triangulation. Furthermore, in order to minimize the distortion of the
L154@P4: decision boundary of the entire set it was advocated that the proximity graphs employed should be sub-graphs of the Delaunay triangulation, such as Gabriel graphs
L155@P4: and relative neighborhood graphs [24]. It was found experimentally that Gabriel
L156@P4: graphs discarded a significantly greater number of data points without degrading the

L158@P4: probability of misclassification. For this reason minimum spanning trees (which are

L176@P5: hybrid algorithm. No practically efficient algorithm exists for computing the Gabriel

L187@P5: point may be computed in O(dk log n) time.

L208@P6: 4 Experiments and Results
L209@P6: The primary goal of this research project was to test the efficacy of the proximity
L210@P6: graphs and their scalability with respect to their edge-density, rather than the running
L211@P6: time of the algorithms used. For this reason, the k-NN, Gabriel, RNG, and MST decision rules were implemented using exact rather than approximate methods such as
L212@P6: GSASH. Another drawback of using GSASH is that it puts a constraint on the maximum number of approximate neighbors it can return (to achieve computational efficiency). In contrast, our goal was to investigate the true error rates that the proximity
L213@P6: graphs can deliver, as well as the number of neighbors required. For this, an exact
L214@P6: approach was needed. In the following, the terms “point” and “instance” are used
L215@P6: interchangeably.
L216@P6: For the k-NN, Gabriel, RNG, and MST decision rules, the voting neighbors of a
L217@P6: query point were first calculated. Then the query point was classified by taking an unweighted majority vote of the voting neighbors' class memberships. Ties were broken
L218@P6: arbitrarily by selecting the class with the smallest index value. The distances between
L219@P6: pairs of instances were computed using the Hybrid Value Difference Metric (HVDM)
L220@P6: described by Wilson and Martinez [27]. This metric allows the handling of both realvalued and categorical attributes, and provides approximate normalization between
L221@P6: the different attributes.
L222@P6: The algorithm for the k-NN rule simply found the k nearest neighbors of the query
L223@P6: point, by computing the distance to every point in the data set, and keeping the k
L224@P6: smallest distances seen so far. No fancy data structure for computing neighbors more
L225@P6: efficiently was used. In our implementation the time complexity of finding the k nearest neighbors of each point was O((k+d)n), where n is the number of points, and d is

1. Introduction
Graphs are basic combinatorial structures, and transformations of structures are fundamental to the development of
mathematics. Particularly, in graph theory, some elementary transformations generate a new graph from an original one
by some simple local changes, such as addition or deletion of a vertex or of an edge, merging and splitting of vertices, edge
contraction, etc. Other advanced transformations create a new graph from the original one by complex changes, such as
complement graph, line graph, total graph, graph power, dual graph, strong resolving graph, etc.
Some of these transformations of graphs emerged as a natural tool to solve practical problems. In other cases, the problem
of finding a specific parameter of a graph has become the problem of finding another parameter of another graph obtained
from the original one. This is the case of the strong resolving graph GSR of a connected graph G which was introduced in [33]
as a tool to study the strong metric dimension of G. Basically, it was shown that the problem of finding the strong metric
dimension of G can be transformed to the problem of finding the vertex cover number of GSR. Since then, several articles
dealing with the strong resolving graph have been published. However, in almost all these works the results related to the
strong resolving graph are not explicit, as they implicitly appear as a part of the proofs of main results concerning the strong
metric dimension. In this sense, this interesting construction has passed in front of researchers’s eyes without the attention
that should require. In this paper, we would like to motivate the graph theory community to have a deeper look into this
graph transformation. Accordingly, herein we survey the state of knowledge on the strong resolving graph and also derive
some new results.

Title: Strong resolving graph of the intersection graph in commutative rings
Authors: E. Dodongeh, A. Moussavi, R. Nikandish
Date: Sat Sep 23 06:51:44 2023

The intersection graph of ideals associated with a commutative unitary ring $R$ is the graph $G(R)$ whose vertices all non-trivial ideals of $R$ and there exists an edge between distinct vertices if and only if the intersection of them is non-zero. In this paper, the structure of the resolving graph of $G(R)$ is characterized and as an application, we evaluate the strong metric dimension of $G(R)$.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
